title: Live-cell imaging of mitochondrial dynamics in Drosophila oenocytes
author: Kumar, Bai

steps.title: Maintain fly cultures and collect females
steps.instruction: Maintain Drosophila melanogaster at 25 °C and 60 % humidity on standard cornmeal–yeast–agar food; collect newly eclosed mixed‑sex flies within 24 h, separate females and males, and use age‑matched, recently mated females for imaging; monitor fly health daily, avoiding overcrowding and contamination.

substeps.instruction: Maintain cultures at 25 °C, 60 % humidity on standard food.
Collect newly eclosed flies within 24 h and separate sexes.
Select age‑matched, recently mated females for experiments.
Monitor health daily, ensuring no overcrowding or contamination.

steps.title: Prepare RU486 food and induce expression
steps.instruction: Prepare RU486‑supplemented food containing 200 µM RU486 in standard food, make fresh weekly and store at 4 °C protected from light for up to 7 days (do not use older than 2 weeks); transfer flies to this food for 3 days to induce mitoGFP expression in oenocytes via PromE‑GeneSwitch‑GAL4; handle RU486 with PPE (lab coat, nitrile gloves, mask) in a fume hood and dispose waste according to safety guidelines.

substeps.instruction: Dissolve RU486 to 200 µM in standard food; prepare fresh weekly.
Store RU486 food at 4 °C protected from light (max 7 days).
Transfer flies to RU486 food for 3 days to induce mitoGFP.
Use PPE (lab coat, nitrile gloves, mask) and work in a fume hood; dispose of RU486 waste safely.

steps.title: Set up confocal microscope for GFP
steps.instruction: Turn on the confocal microscope (e.g., Olympus FV3000) and allow lasers/electronics to warm up for at least 30 min; clean objective lenses with lens paper and cleaning solution; calibrate GFP detection (488 nm excitation, 500–550 nm emission); enable autofocus for long time‑lapse imaging (up to 90 min).

substeps.instruction: Power on the microscope and warm up for ≥30 min.
Clean objective lenses with lens paper and cleaning solution.
Calibrate for GFP: 488 nm excitation, 500–550 nm emission.
Enable autofocus to maintain focus during up to 90‑min time‑lapse.

steps.title: Prepare paraquat stock and working solution
steps.instruction: Dissolve paraquat dichloride in Schneider’s Drosophila Medium to make a 1 M stock solution; store the stock at 4 °C protected from light for 2–4 weeks (discard if older than 4 weeks); immediately before use dilute the stock to a 600 µM working concentration; protect all paraquat solutions from light; handle paraquat in a certified fume hood with PPE (lab coat, nitrile gloves, safety mask/eye protection) and dispose waste according to hazardous chemical regulations.

substeps.instruction: Make 1 M paraquat stock in Schneider’s Drosophila Medium.
Store stock at 4 °C protected from light for 2–4 weeks; discard if >4 weeks old.
Dilute stock to 600 µM working solution immediately before use.
Handle paraquat in a fume hood with PPE and dispose of waste safely.

description: Mitochondria are highly dynamic organelles whose morphology reflects a balance between fission and fusion. These processes are essential for maintaining cellular homeostasis, and their dysregulation contributes to aging and disease.1,2 While live-cell imaging of mitochondrial dynamics has been successfully demonstrated in Drosophila embryos3,4; and larvae,5,6 there is currently no established protocol for performing live-cell or time-lapse imaging in adult Drosophila oenocytes. Adult tissues present unique challenges, including cuticle opacity, tissue movement, and difficulties in maintaining tissue viability during imaging. This protocol describes a detailed workflow to prepare adult flies expressing mitoGFP in oenocytes, dissect the abdominal cuticle to expose intact oenocytes, and mount the tissue for stable time-lapse confocal imaging. The method enables visualization of mitochondrial morphology and dynamics for up to 90 minutes under near-physiological conditions. As a demonstration, we show that paraquat (PQ) treatment induces mitochondrial fission in oenocytes, indicating oxidative stress–mediated mitochondrial remodeling. In our associated research, we further used this protocol to compare mitochondrial dynamics between young and old flies, revealing age-associated inhibition of mitochondrial fission.7 This protocol focuses on adult oenocytes, hepatocyte-like cells involved in lipid metabolism and detoxification, but the workflow can be adapted to other tissues located beneath or attached to the abdominal cuticle, such as the fat body or abdominal muscles, with minor modifications. Media preparation, RU486 induction, and PQ stock solutions should be completed before beginning dissections and imaging.
